verdict.reasoning: Patient says, “terrible headaches since midday on the left side… I guess it's throbbing on that left side,” confirming left-sided throbbing headache since midday.
Doctor asks if pain was sudden or gradual; patient replies, “No, really, it just happened,” indicating sudden onset.
Patient states, “I noticed some zigzag lines in my vision. A few minutes before the headache started,” linking zigzag lines in vision with the headache.
Doctor asks if blurred vision is both eyes or just left; patient responds, “It feels like it's on both,” confirming blurred vision in both eyes.
Patient says, “I just feel like I need to vomit” and later “I vomited twice,” indicating nausea associated with the headache.
Doctor asks about bright lights; patient replies, “I'm wearing sunglasses right now. You know, light's really hurting my eyes,” which is photophobia.
Doctor asks about vomiting and patient replies, “Yeah, I vomited twice,” referring to the current episode.
Patient says, “I did have a similar headache a few weeks ago… For a couple of days,” confirming prior similar headache lasting a couple of days.
Doctor asks, “Have you had any injuries to your head? Have you had a fall recently or been knocked on the head?” Patient replies, “No,” indicating no recent head trauma.
Doctor asks if anyone has told her she has had migraines; patient answers, “No,” and also says she’s “not been diagnosed,” indicating no prior migraine history.
Patient states, “I take the pill, microgynon.” Doctor asks duration and indication; patient answers, “Three months… It's for contraception.”
Patient says, “My mum had. Has migraines,” confirming maternal history of migraines.
Patient adds, “My mum has an underactive thyroid as well,” confirming this family history.
Patient says, “working fashion industry and you know, they're wondering what's going on,” confirming employment in fashion industry.
Patient describes job as “really stressful, actually. Having problems with like people at work… managers like putting a lot of pressure on me,” indicating high work stress.
Doctor asks, “Is it getting you down?” Patient replies, “I don't feel down. Just feel a bit stressed,” indicating she does not report depression.
In response to “Who's at home with you?” patient says, “I live on my own,” confirming she lives alone.
Patient responds “No” to “Do you smoke at all?” and “No” to “Do you drink much in the way of alcohol?” indicating no smoking or alcohol use.
Doctor asks about fevers; patient replies, “No, I don't feel feverish,” indicating no fever.
Doctor asks, “Any other funny skin rashes…?” Patient says, “No, I haven't noticed anything like that,” indicating no rashes.
Doctor asks, “Have you noticed any problems with your speech at all?” Patient replies, “No,” confirming no speech difficulty.
Doctor asks, “Any problems with your arms and legs, for example, numbness or weakness?” Patient replies, “No,” indicating no limb weakness or numbness.
Doctor asks, “Any difficulty with balance, your balance or coordination?” Patient replies, “No,” indicating no balance issues.
Doctor says, “I wonder whether you may. May have a migraine. Migraine type headache. It sounds very classical of that nature,” making suspected migraine the primary assessment.

Doctor states, “The headache on one side, throbbing nature, the nausea, vomiting, sensitive to bright lights,” explicitly linking these features (left-sided throbbing, nausea/vomiting, photophobia) as suggesting migraine.
Doctor explores work being “quite stressful” and patient describes significant work stress; this is part of the assessment of her situation.
Although work stress is discussed, the doctor never explicitly states that stress is possibly contributing to the headache; this causal link is not made in the transcript.
Doctor says, “I think keeping a headache diary will be quite important to see exactly what's triggering these headaches,” advising a headache diary for triggers.
Doctor advises, “Some strong painkillers would be advisable. So, you know, think about paracetamol or even cocodamol and some anti inflammatories such as ibuprofen and naproxen.”

Doctor says, “if your headaches were to become more persistent, then we can maybe think about giving you some medications that will stop your headaches from happening in the first place. Something prophylactic medicines.”

Doctor instructs, “if your symptoms aren't getting better… or indeed they're getting worse… if your headache's getting worse… or you develop any weakness in your arms and legs or your vision, then I want you to come back and see me straight away,” which is return if worsening or new neurological symptoms.
